reasoningSteps: Model and boundary: an invented model assigns probability 0.5 to each of 1,000 independent events that actually happened, and separately predicts the probability that one email is spam. Natural logarithms are used; a different base only rescales the results.

Derivation: the joint probability is 0.5^1000 ≈ 9.33 × 10^−302, close to the smallest normal number the IEEE double-precision format can hold (about 2.2 × 10^−308), and with 1,100 events the product underflows to 0. Because log(ab) = log a + log b, the logarithm of the product is the sum 1,000 × ln 0.5 ≈ −693.15, an ordinary number.

Independent check: a logarithm answers the inverse question of exponentiation, so e^−0.105 ≈ 0.90 recovers the probability behind a loss of 0.105, and e^4.605 ≈ 100 shows that a loss of 4.605 corresponds to a probability of 1/100.

Misconception to reject: 'log loss is just the error rate.' It scores the probability given to the true outcome: for a spam email, predicting 0.9 costs −ln 0.9 ≈ 0.105, predicting 0.5 costs ≈ 0.693 and predicting 0.01 costs ≈ 4.605, about 44 times the confident correct prediction.

Change one factor: measure in bits with base-2 logarithms. The confident wrong prediction then costs −log₂ 0.01 ≈ 6.644 bits instead of 4.605; every loss is multiplied by the same factor, 1 / ln 2, so rankings between models do not change.

Source and limits: scikit-learn's guide to metrics and scoring defines the per-sample log loss for a true label y in {0, 1} and estimated probability p as −(y log p + (1 − y) log(1 − p)), the negative log-likelihood: https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/model_evaluation.html. The probabilities here are invented.

reasoningSteps: Model and boundary: an idealized planar arm with its base at the origin. The shoulder angle θ1 is measured from the x-axis, the elbow angle θ2 from the first link, and the links are 0.5 m and 0.3 m long. Real arms add joint offsets, limits and flexing that this model ignores.

Derivation: each link contributes its length times the cosine of its absolute angle to x, and times the sine to y. The second link points at θ1 + θ2 = 75°. So x = 0.5 cos 30° + 0.3 cos 75° ≈ 0.433 + 0.078 = 0.511 m and y = 0.5 sin 30° + 0.3 sin 75° ≈ 0.250 + 0.290 = 0.540 m.

Independent check: the distance from the base to the gripper follows from the law of cosines, r² = 0.5² + 0.3² + 2 × 0.5 × 0.3 × cos 45° ≈ 0.5521, so r ≈ 0.743 m, and the coordinates give √(0.511² + 0.540²) ≈ 0.743 m as well. For the first link alone, (0.5 cos 30°)² + (0.5 sin 30°)² = 0.25 = 0.5², which is the identity cos²t + sin²t = 1 scaled by the length squared.

Misconception to reject: 'the angle can go into the code as 30.' Most math libraries take radians, so 30° must be passed as π/6 ≈ 0.5236. Passing 30 directly computes cos(30 rad) ≈ 0.154 and sin(30 rad) ≈ −0.988 and places the gripper at about (0.354, −0.610) m, below the base, which is a common real bug.

Change one factor: set the shoulder to 390° instead of 30°. Sine and cosine repeat every 360°, so every term, and the gripper position, is unchanged; the arm cannot tell the two commands apart, although a controller that counts full turns must. With the elbow straight (θ2 = 0°), the reach becomes 0.8 m and the gripper sits at about (0.693, 0.400) m.

Source and limits: OpenStax Algebra and Trigonometry, section 7.3 'Unit Circle', defines cos t and sin t as the x- and y-coordinates of the point on the unit circle at angle t and states the identity cos²t + sin²t = 1: https://openstax.org/books/algebra-and-trigonometry/pages/7-3-unit-circle. Scaling those coordinates by each link's length gives the arm equations used here; the arm itself is invented.
